questions.stem: What is an invasive species?
options: A native predator that keeps the numbers of its prey species in check
A species that migrates between two different ecosystems each year
A non-native species that spreads and harms its new ecosystem
A native species whose population has fallen to very low numbers in the wild
questions.explanation: Invasive species are introduced from elsewhere, establish and spread, and damage native species or ecosystem processes. A native species in decline is threatened, not invasive.

questions.stem: Cane toads were released in Queensland in 1935 to control beetles in sugar cane. Why have they caused declines in native predators such as northern quolls and goannas?
options: They outcompete the predators for nectar from native flowering plants
They carry a virus that infects marsupial and reptile predators only
They eat the eggs of the native predators in their nests and burrows
Predators that eat them are poisoned by toxins in their skin
questions.explanation: Cane toads have toxin-producing glands, and native predators that have not evolved with them die after eating toads. Toads failed to control the cane beetles they were introduced for.

questions.stem: European rabbits in Australia graze native plants and dig extensive warrens. Which ecosystem change is most likely where rabbits are abundant?
options: Loss of ground cover, erosion and less food for native herbivores
More native seedlings, because rabbits carry seeds into new areas
Fewer foxes, because rabbits compete with them for the same food
Richer soil, because rabbits fix nitrogen from the air in their gut
questions.explanation: Rabbits eat seedlings and ground plants, compete with native herbivores and loosen soil, which leads to erosion and prevents plant regeneration. They are prey for foxes, so they tend to support fox numbers.

questions.stem: Sites where red foxes were baited had four times as many small native mammals after five years as unbaited sites with similar habitat. What do these data suggest?
options: Foxes were absent from the unbaited sites during the study
Fox predation was limiting small native mammal populations
Baiting directly raised the birth rate of small native mammals
Small native mammals prefer to move into recently baited sites
questions.explanation: With habitat matched, the main difference between sites is fox control, so the higher mammal numbers suggest that foxes were holding populations down. The data do not show how the increase happened, such as through births or migration.

questions.stem: Why does replacing natural vegetation with a monoculture reduce the health of an ecosystem?
options: It stops pests from finding the crop because there is so much of it
It swaps varied habitat for one species, cutting food and shelter
It increases the genetic diversity of the crop species that is being grown
It adds nutrients to the soil because one species uses fewer of them
questions.explanation: A single crop provides few niches, so many native species lose food and shelter, and the uniform crop is prone to pest and disease outbreaks. Monocultures are usually genetically uniform, not diverse.

questions.stem: An insecticide sprayed on crops is found at rising concentrations in insects, then small birds, then birds of prey. What is this process, and why are top predators most affected?
options: Biomagnification; top predators are the only animals sensitive to it
Bioremediation; microbes convert the chemical into more toxic products
Biomagnification; the chemical builds up in tissues at each trophic level
Eutrophication; extra nutrients cause algal blooms that starve predators
questions.explanation: Persistent chemicals are stored in body tissue rather than excreted, so each predator accumulates the amount from all the prey it eats, and the concentration is highest at the top of the food chain. Other animals are also affected, but at lower doses.

questions.stem: Land clearing breaks a large forest into small, isolated patches. Which effect on the populations living there is most likely?
options: Greater genetic diversity, because each patch now evolves separately
Faster gene flow, because animals must travel further between patches
Smaller, isolated populations with less gene flow
Larger populations, because animals crowd into the patches that remain
questions.explanation: Fragmentation reduces habitat area and cuts movement between patches, so populations become small, inbred and vulnerable to chance events. Isolated populations lose alleles by drift faster than they gain them.

questions.stem: Koalas in New South Wales have been listed as endangered. Which set of natural and human-induced causes best explains their decline?
options: Cold winters, competition with possums for burrows and hunting by cane toads
Clearing, bushfires, drought, chlamydia and vehicle strikes
Competition with rabbits for eucalyptus leaves and hunting by wedge-tailed eagles
Overgrazing by kangaroos and the loss of insect prey through pesticide spraying
questions.explanation: Koalas depend on eucalypt habitat, which is lost to clearing and fire, while drought, chlamydia and cars and dogs add to deaths. Koalas eat eucalyptus leaves rather than insects, and rabbits do not compete with them for leaves.

questions.stem: The southern cassowary of north Queensland eats fruit and disperses the seeds of many rainforest plants, some of which depend almost entirely on it. Why is it described as a keystone species?
options: It is the most numerous animal in the rainforest, so it makes up most of the animal biomass
It is the top predator in the rainforest, so it controls the numbers of all the herbivores
It is the only animal in the rainforest that eats fruit, so it has no competitors at all
Its effect is large relative to its numbers, so its loss would change the forest
questions.explanation: A keystone species has an effect far out of proportion to its abundance; without cassowaries, some large-seeded plants would not be dispersed and forest composition would change. Keystone species are not necessarily numerous or predators.

questions.stem: Data show that a large native predator suppresses foxes and feral cats, and that small native mammals are scarce where the predator is absent. What is the most likely result of removing the predator from an ecosystem?
options: Fox and cat numbers rise, and small native mammals decline
Small native mammals increase, because a predator has gone
Foxes and cats decline, because the predator left them food
Plants are lost at once, because the predator ate seedlings
questions.explanation: Removing a top predator releases smaller predators from control, and these then eat more small mammals; this is called mesopredator release. The small mammals are not the large predator's main prey in these data, so they lose rather than gain.

questions.stem: Which is the best description of biodiversity?
options: The variety of genes, species and ecosystems
The number of individuals of one species in an area
The total mass of all living things in an ecosystem
The number of trophic levels in a food web
questions.explanation: Biodiversity includes genetic diversity within species, species diversity within ecosystems and the diversity of ecosystems themselves. Population size and biomass are different measures.

questions.stem: Two forests each contain 20 tree species. In forest A one species makes up 90% of the trees; in forest B the species occur in similar numbers. Which statement is correct?
options: Both forests have equal species diversity because they have the same richness
Forest A has greater species diversity because one species dominates it
Species diversity depends only on the total number of trees in the forest
Forest B has greater species diversity because its species are more even
questions.explanation: Species diversity takes account of both richness (number of species) and evenness (how equally individuals are spread among them). With the same richness, the more even forest is more diverse.

questions.stem: A population of 30 animals has lost most of its genetic diversity. Which problem is it most likely to face?
options: Higher fertility, because mates are closely related and compatible
Inbreeding, with more offspring homozygous for harmful recessive alleles
Faster adaptation, because once-rare alleles have now become common
A larger gene pool, because fewer alleles compete within each individual
questions.explanation: In a small population, mates are often relatives who share alleles, so harmful recessive alleles are more often inherited in pairs, reducing survival and fertility. Low diversity also reduces the capacity to adapt.

questions.stem: Strawberry plants spread by runners and also produce seeds after pollination. Which comparison is correct?
options: Runners produce clones of the parent; seeds produce genetically varied offspring
Runners produce genetically varied offspring; seeds produce clones of the parent
Runners and seeds both produce offspring identical to the parent plant
Runners and seeds both produce offspring that combine alleles of two parents
questions.explanation: Runners are asexual, growing new plants by mitosis, so they are genetically identical to the parent. Seeds result from fertilisation, so they combine alleles from two gametes and vary.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares external and internal fertilisation?
options: External fertilisation releases huge numbers of gametes but few young survive; internal gives fewer, better-protected young
Internal fertilisation releases huge numbers of gametes but few young survive; external gives fewer, better-protected young
External fertilisation happens only on land and internal fertilisation happens only in water
Internal fertilisation produces clones of the parent; external fertilisation produces varied offspring
questions.explanation: Animals such as many fish, frogs and corals release many gametes into water, where most are lost, while internal fertilisation in mammals, birds and reptiles gives fewer offspring with more protection. Both are sexual, so both produce varied offspring.

questions.stem: On a reef, many corals release their eggs and sperm into the water on the same nights. How can this broadcast spawning increase variation among the offspring?
options: The seawater causes a mutation in every gamete before fertilisation
Gametes from many parents mix, so many combinations of alleles are possible
Each egg can be fertilised only by sperm released by the same parent coral
The eggs develop without fertilisation, so each larva is a clone
questions.explanation: When many colonies spawn together, eggs can be fertilised by sperm from many different colonies, so offspring carry many combinations of alleles. Synchronised spawning also improves the chance of fertilisation.

questions.stem: Which pairing of an asexual reproduction method and an organism is correct?
options: Budding: ferns
Parthenogenesis: bacteria
Binary fission: bacteria
Spore formation: hydra
questions.explanation: Bacteria divide by binary fission. Hydra reproduce by budding, ferns by spores, and parthenogenesis, development from an unfertilised egg, occurs in some insects and reptiles.

questions.stem: A fungus reproduces asexually by spores while conditions are favourable. Why could the population be at risk if its environment changes quickly?
options: Its offspring are identical, so few may suit the new conditions
Spores are destroyed by any change in temperature or moisture in the environment
Asexual reproduction stops as soon as the environment begins to change
Spores carry more mutations than sexual offspring, so most of them die
questions.explanation: Asexual reproduction copies a genotype that suits current conditions, but a population of clones has little variation for selection to act on when conditions change. Spores are often resistant structures, so they are not destroyed by small changes.

questions.stem: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission and can double in number every 20 minutes in good conditions. How can a population of bacteria adapt quickly to a change, even though it produces clones?
options: Every cell formed by binary fission is resistant to any new condition
Huge numbers and short generations let rare mutations arise and spread fast
Binary fission mixes the alleles of two parent cells in every new cell
Each cell changes its own genes during its lifetime to suit the change
questions.explanation: Each division carries a small chance of mutation, and with billions of cells and rapid generations, a beneficial mutation is likely to appear and can quickly increase by selection, as with antibiotic resistance. Individual cells do not change their genes on purpose.

questions.stem: What is the founder effect?
options: Loss of alleles when a disaster kills most of a population at random
Movement of alleles from one population into another by migration
Increase of alleles that suit the conditions of a new environment
Genetic drift when a few individuals found a new population
questions.explanation: A small founding group carries a non-representative sample of the source population's alleles, so allele frequencies in the new population differ by chance. A random disaster that shrinks an existing population is a bottleneck.

questions.stem: A species is hunted until only a few dozen individuals remain, then recovers to thousands. Why does it still have low genetic diversity?
options: Populations that are recovering always mutate more slowly than other populations
The hunters selectively removed every individual carrying a recessive allele
Large populations lose alleles by genetic drift faster than small ones do
The bottleneck lost most alleles, and regrowth only multiplied the rest
questions.explanation: A bottleneck leaves only the alleles carried by the survivors, and regrowth increases numbers without restoring lost alleles, which return only slowly by mutation or gene flow. Drift is stronger in small populations, not large ones.

questions.stem: What effect does gene flow usually have on two populations of the same species?
options: It makes their allele frequencies more similar
It makes their allele frequencies more different
It removes all variation from both populations
It splits them into two species within a few generations
questions.explanation: Gene flow moves alleles between populations through migration or the spread of gametes such as pollen, so it evens out their allele frequencies and works against speciation.

questions.stem: To model drift, students put 50 red and 50 white beads in a bag. They draw 10 beads at random, make a new bag with the same colour proportions, and repeat for many generations. What are they most likely to observe?
options: Red beads always increase because they were placed in the bag first
Both colours increase in number each generation as the bag refills
The proportions change randomly, and one colour may be lost completely
The proportions stay exactly at 50% red and 50% white every generation
questions.explanation: Drawing only 10 beads gives large chance differences from 50 : 50, and these carry forward, so frequencies wander and one allele can become fixed. The small sample size is what makes drift strong.

questions.stem: In a population of 500 moths, 80 are bb, 220 are Bb and 200 are BB. What is the frequency of allele b?
questions.explanation: There are 1000 alleles in total. The b alleles number 2 x 80 + 220 = 380, so the frequency of b is 380 / 1000 = 0.38. The figure 0.62 is the frequency of B.

questions.stem: Peahens choose to mate with peacocks that have the largest tail displays. What effect does this non-random mating have on allele frequencies?
options: Alleles for large tails are lost from the population by drift
Female choice causes new mutations for larger tails to appear
Alleles linked to large tails increase in frequency over generations
All alleles in the population stay at the same frequencies
questions.explanation: Males with large tails leave more offspring, so alleles associated with large tails become more common; this is sexual selection, a form of non-random mating. Mate choice does not cause mutations.

questions.stem: A population's genetic diversity has fallen steadily over 50 years. How is this most likely to affect the population?
options: It gains new alleles more quickly because fewer alleles remain
It becomes more resistant to disease because it is more uniform
It becomes less able to adapt to new diseases or a changing climate
It becomes more stable because its individuals are more similar
questions.explanation: Variation is the raw material for natural selection; with fewer variants, it is less likely that some individuals can survive a new pathogen or condition, so the population is less stable and at greater risk of extinction.

questions.stem: Devil facial tumour disease spreads when Tasmanian devils bite each other, transferring living cancer cells. Why do these tumour cells usually escape the new host's immune system?
options: Devils have no adaptive immune system, so they cannot recognise any cells
The tumour cells are coated in antibodies made by the first infected devil
Low MHC gene diversity means the tumour cells do not appear foreign
The tumour cells are viruses that are too small for immune cells to detect
questions.explanation: Low genetic diversity, including in the MHC genes that mark cells as self, means the tumour cells look similar to the host's own cells and are not rejected. The disease is a transmissible cancer, not a virus.

questions.stem: Some Tasmanian devil populations exposed to facial tumour disease for many years now show higher frequencies of certain alleles linked to immune function. What does this suggest?
options: Healthy devils from a captive population replaced all of the local devils
Natural selection is acting on the variation that remains in the population
The disease caused the devils to develop the new alleles that they needed
Genetic drift alone has raised the frequency of every immune-related allele
questions.explanation: Devils with alleles that improve survival leave more offspring, so those alleles rise in frequency, which is natural selection. The alleles were already present; the disease did not create them.

questions.stem: Why have healthy Tasmanian devils been kept in disease-free insurance populations, including one on Maria Island?
options: To give the tumour time to evolve into a harmless form in the wild
To breed devils that are all clones of one disease-resistant animal
To increase inbreeding so that recessive resistance alleles appear
To keep a disease-free population with high genetic diversity
questions.explanation: Insurance populations protect the species from extinction and are managed to retain as much of the remaining genetic diversity as possible for future release. Inbreeding and cloning would reduce diversity further.

questions.stem: When a fungus infects a leaf, plant cells around the site of infection quickly die. How does this hypersensitive response help the plant?
options: It feeds the fungus so that it stays in one place
It releases antibodies that bind to the fungal cells
It lets the rest of the leaf photosynthesise faster
It deprives the pathogen of living cells
questions.explanation: Many pathogens need living host cells, so killing cells around the infection isolates the pathogen and stops its spread. Plants do not make antibodies.

questions.stem: Which is a chemical response of a plant to a pathogen?
options: Forming tyloses that plug the xylem vessels
Producing antimicrobial compounds called phytoalexins
Thickening cell walls with callose and lignin
Closing stomata to block the entry of bacteria
questions.explanation: Phytoalexins are antimicrobial chemicals made in response to infection. Thickened cell walls, closed stomata and tyloses are physical barriers.

questions.stem: What causes Panama disease of bananas?
options: A virus carried by aphids that feed on the young banana leaves
A bacterium spread by bees that visit the banana flowers
A nematode worm that feeds on the fruit as it ripens
A soil-borne fungus that invades the roots and blocks the xylem
questions.explanation: Panama disease is caused by the fungus Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense, which lives in soil, enters through the roots and grows in the xylem. The Tropical Race 4 strain attacks Cavendish bananas.

questions.stem: A student cuts across the stems of banana plants infected with Panama disease and sees brown discoloured vessels. Why do infected plants wilt and yellow?
options: The fungus digests the chloroplasts inside the leaf cells
The fungus stops the roots from producing root hairs
The fungus forces all of the stomata to stay open
The fungus blocks the xylem, so water cannot reach the leaves
questions.explanation: The fungus grows in the water-conducting xylem, and the plant's own responses also plug the vessels, so water flow to the leaves fails and they wilt and yellow.

questions.stem: Why do banana farms in regions with Panama disease require visitors to clean their footwear and vehicles?
options: Cleaning destroys the virus that causes the disease
The fungus survives in soil carried on shoes
The fungus is carried by insects that rest on shoes
The fungus produces airborne spores only on rubber
questions.explanation: Panama disease spreads through infested soil, water and plant material, and its spores survive in soil for decades, so cleaning off soil is a key biosecurity step. It is caused by a fungus, not a virus.

questions.stem: Myrtle rust, a fungal disease first found in Australia in 2010, infects the new growth of plants in the myrtle family. Which ecosystem effect is most likely?
options: Increase in genetic diversity of myrtles, because the rust adds new genes
Decline only of introduced garden plants, leaving native forests unharmed
Decline of susceptible native species and the animals that depend on them
Increase in all myrtle species, because the rust prunes their old growth
questions.explanation: Myrtle rust attacks many native plants in the myrtle family, and highly susceptible species have declined sharply, affecting the insects, birds and other animals that rely on them. Pathogens do not add genes to their hosts.

questions.stem: Stonefly and mayfly nymphs are sensitive to pollution, while some worms tolerate it. A survey finds many nymphs upstream of a factory, but downstream only worms. What does this indicate?
options: The worms have eaten the nymphs downstream
Water quality is poorer downstream of the factory
Water quality is better downstream of the factory
The nymphs have migrated downstream to feed
questions.explanation: The absence of pollution-sensitive indicators below the factory, while they thrive above it, points to pollution from the factory. Tolerant species alone do not show good water quality.

questions.stem: Which feature makes a species a good indicator of change in an ecosystem?
options: It migrates long distances away from the ecosystem each year
It is sensitive to a specific condition and easy to sample and identify
It tolerates a very wide range of conditions throughout its habitat
It is extremely rare and hard to find in the ecosystem
questions.explanation: An indicator species responds clearly and predictably to a particular change, such as pollution or habitat loss, and can be surveyed reliably. A species that tolerates everything shows nothing about change.

questions.stem: Why is ecosystem diversity, as well as genetic and species diversity, important for the continuity of life?
options: A single large ecosystem type supports the greatest number of species
More ecosystems house more species and buffer against any one's loss
Ecosystems with more diversity always contain fewer species in total
Ecosystem diversity prevents species from evolving to new conditions
questions.explanation: A range of ecosystems provides more habitats and niches, so more species persist, and if one ecosystem is damaged, others remain as refuges and sources for recovery. Diversity at every level makes life more resilient to change.
